chapter_theme: Justice as the root of a king's power: the people live by his sceptre as the world lives by rain, and it wins him battles, brings rain and protects him in turn. The chapter ends by defending punishment, even death, as part of just rule.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the definition of just rule (541), its distinction (542-543), the fruits for one who keeps it (544-547), the ruin of one who doesn't (548), and punishment as no fault (549-550).

541.reading: To investigate, show no favour to anyone, hold to what is fitting for a ruler and act after consideration: that is justice.
541.nuance: The definition is mainly procedural, four steps with no mention of outcome. கண்ணோடாது is a strong word for a book with a whole chapter praising கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar extends யார்மாட்டும் to those dearer than life, and Manakkudavar to one's own kin.

542.reading: All the world lives looking to the sky; the people live looking to the ruler's sceptre.
542.nuance: நோக்கி has the sense of dependence as well as looking up. Parimelazhagar narrows the point: the sky gives food and the sceptre gives security, and without security the food is no use to the people. So the sceptre is the more basic of the two for them.

543.reading: The ruler's sceptre stands as the origin of the books of the அந்தணர் and of virtue.
543.nuance: ஆதி is a bold word. It makes politics the source of learning and morals, the opposite of what might be expected. Parimelazhagar notices this, because the Vedas are eternal for him, and explains ஆதி as meaning they don't function without the sceptre.

positions.position: அந்தணர் நூல் is the Veda: beginningless itself, but it needs the sceptre in order to operate.
positions.quote: வேதமும் அறனும் - அநாதியாயினும், செங்கோல் இல்வழி நடவா ஆகலின்,

positions.position: They are books of the virtuous, with no reference to the Veda or to Brahmins.
positions.quote: ஓர் அரசின் செங்கோன்மைதான் அறவோர் நூல்களுக்கும் அறவழிச் செயல்களுக்கும் அடிப்படையாக அமையும்.

544.reading: The world stands embracing the feet of the great ruler who embraces his people and wields the sceptre.
544.nuance: The same word தழீஇ appears twice, and the reciprocity is the point: the king embraces his people and the world embraces his feet. The embrace from above must come first.

545.reading: Rain and harvest gather together in the land of the ruler who wields the sceptre according to its nature.

positions.position: It is a literal effect: sky and earth work together and yield abundance where rule is just.
positions.quote: வானும் நிலனும் சேரத் தொழிற்பட்டு வளம் சுரக்கும் என்பதாம்.

positions.position: It is a comparison: just government is like seasonal rain and a fine harvest.
positions.quote: பெய்யும் மழையினால் வளமான விளைச்சல் கிடைப்பதற்கு ஒப்பானதாகும்.

546.reading: It is not the spear that gives victory but the ruler's sceptre, if it doesn't bend.
546.nuance: வேல் and கோல் rhyme and look alike as long shafts. The comparison also lets the sceptre be read as itself a weapon. The verse makes the claim without saying how justice wins battles. Parimelazhagar only says a spear strikes true when the sceptre is straight, and quotes a Sangam poem in support.

547.reading: The ruler guards all the world; justice guards him, if he doesn't falter in it.
547.nuance: முட்டாச் செயின் means even when it costs. Parimelazhagar's examples are the most extreme ones in Tamil memory: the king who gave judgment on his own son and the king who cut off his own hand, both from the Silappatikaram. That shows what 'not faltering' is taken to require.

548.reading: A ruler who isn't easily approached and who doesn't examine and do justice falls low and perishes by himself.
548.nuance: தானே கெடும் is close to 448: the ruin needs no enemy. Parimelazhagar's 'low state' is sin and blame, and he supports it by quoting that virtue is death to those who have done wrong.

549.reading: Guarding the people, caring for them and removing wrongdoing are no stain on a king: they are his work.
549.nuance: வடு அன்று answers a charge that must have been in the air. Parimelazhagar makes it explicit: punishing one's subjects could seem against virtue, and he replies that purifying them of wrong is the king's caste duty.

550.reading: A king's dealing with the cruel by death is equal to weeding out the young crop.
550.nuance: The weeding image makes killing seem an act of care for the crop. It says nothing about who decides which are the weeds, and the next chapter opens on a king who may be one.

positions.position: The king is to punish by death those who burn, poison, rob, and those who desire another's wife. Not doing so harms the world.
positions.quote: அரசன் கொடியவர்களைக் கொலையான் ஒறுத்துத் தக்கோரைக் காத்தல்;

positions.position: The cruel are a narrower list: thieves, highway robbers and plunderers.
கொலை is the crime and not the penalty: the state simply punishes those who commit murder and similar cruelty.
positions.quote: கொலை முதலிய கொடுமைகள் புரிவோரை, ஓர் அரசு தண்டனைக்குள்ளாக்குவது

links.note: 327 says don't take another's life even if it costs your own. 550 says the king's killing of the cruel is like weeding. The book's sharpest split between Aram and Porul: an absolute rule meets the role of king. Parimelazhagar resolves it through caste duty, which the verses don't mention.

541 makes justice not showing கண்ணோட்டம் to anyone. 578 gives the world to those able to show it without harming the work. So the king both must and must not, and 578's condition, the work unharmed, is the hinge.

528 tells a king not to look at all alike but by rank; 541 says to show no favour to anyone. Household management and the court of justice have different requirements, though they are only two chapters apart.

The chapter on rain calls it the world's nectar because it keeps the world going. 542 gives the sceptre that same place for human society, which is why the failure of one can later cause the other in 559.
30 defines அந்தணர் by compassion toward all life, and not by birth. If that is carried here, 543's அந்தணர் நூல் need not be the Veda, and this gives Kalaignar's reading a basis inside the Kural.

761 calls a fearless army the chief of a king's assets. 546 says it isn't the spear but the sceptre that gives victory. Porul itself has two answers to what wins wars, one in its justice chapter and one in its army chapter.

source_issues: 548: Kalaignar's ஆடம்பரமாகவும் doesn't correspond to எண்பதத்தான் as the other sources read it, so I didn't use it.
